chunks: As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning:
A man performs the whole wudu (ablution) except for his feet, then he enters the water with them forcefully. He said: “That suffices for him.”

So this report is to be understood as applying to a state of taqiyyah. But in the case of free choice, only wiping over them is permissible, as we have explained. If someone says: Why do you deny that the genitive reading in the verse, upon which you relied, does not necessitate wiping, but only indicates that the feet share with the head in grammatical inflection, not that they share in ruling—so that this may be by adjacency, as occurs frequently in Arabic speech, such as their saying: “the ruined lizard-hole,” though “ruined” is a description of the hole, not the lizard, and it is put in the genitive due to adjacency; and as in the poet’s line... and the adjective belongs to another word; and as in the verse of al-Aʿshā... Thus, it would not be objectionable that the feet are washed even if they are in the genitive. We say: this is false for several reasons. First, there is no disagreement among the scholars of Arabic that inflection by adjacency does not extend beyond its limited cases, and what is in this degree of irregularity and departure from principles cannot be used to interpret the speech of Allah, Exalted is He. Second, every place inflected by adjacency among the examples mentioned by the objector and those not mentioned lacks the conjunction that is contained in the verse; and upon that conjunction we relied in establishing the equality of the ruling of the feet and the heads. Even if analogy upon adjacency were acceptable, the verse would still be outside it because it contains the indicator of conjunction that is absent from the places inflected by adjacency. There is no doubt for anyone who understands Arabic that adjacency has no force alongside conjunction. Third, inflection by adjacency is only considered acceptable where ambiguity in meaning is removed. Do you not see that ambiguity is absent in making “ruined” a description of the lizard, since it is known that it is a description of the hole? Likewise, “wrapped” is known to describe the elder, not the cloak. But the verse is not like this, because as for the feet, it is possible for their obligation to be wiping just as it is possible for it to be washing, and doubt in that is possible, not impossible. So adjacency cannot be applied here because of the resulting confusion and ambiguity, and because that would depart from the known usage of the Arabs. As for the line recited from al-Aʿshā, they erred in supposing that there is adjacency there; rather, “thawāʾ” is in the genitive as a substitute for “al-ḥawl,” and the meaning is: ‘Indeed there was in a stay, in which I stayed, the fulfillment of needs’; and this category of substitution is substitution of inclusion.
As He, Exalted, said: “Slain were the companions of the trench — the fire,” and He said: “They ask you about the sacred month: fighting in it.”

If it is said: How do you claim that adjacency has no effect with the conjunction wāw, despite His saying, Exalted is He: “Immortal youths will circulate among them, with cups and pitchers...” up to His saying, “and wide-eyed maidens,” so that their being in the genitive would be by adjacency, since they circulate, and are not themselves circulated around? And similarly the poet’s line... where “bound” is put in the genitive by adjacency though it ought to be nominative. We say: the first thing that invalidates this statement is that not all the reciters read “wa-ḥūrun ʿīnun” in the genitive; rather, most of the seven reciters read it in the nominative. Those who read it in the genitive were Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, and in one narration al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim; and it has also been reported that he recited it in the accusative. There is another explanation for the genitive besides adjacency: when His saying, Exalted is He, ‘Those are the ones brought near, in gardens of bliss’ had preceded, ‘and wide-eyed maidens’ was coordinated to ‘gardens of bliss,’ as though He said: they are in gardens of bliss and in the company or association of the wide-eyed maidens, with the annexed word omitted. This is a fine interpretation mentioned by Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī in al-Ḥujjah fī al-Qirāʾah. As for the poetic line cited by the questioner, it is contrary to what he imagined, because the meaning of ‘There remained none but a captive’ is ‘there remained none other than a captive,’ and then ‘and bound’ is in the genitive by coordination to the meaning and position of ‘captured.’ As for the poet’s line, ‘Are you, if your she-ass dies, a rider to the family of Bisṭām ibn Qays, and an addressee?’ the correct form may be nominative, but the transmitter made it genitive by mistake; or it may be intended as an imperative, and only rendered genitive because of poetic license.
“Immortal youths will circulate among them, with cups and pitchers,” up to His saying: “and wide-eyed maidens,” and His saying, Exalted is He: “Those are the ones brought near, in gardens of bliss.”

If it is said: Why do you deny, while accepting that the verse establishes wiping of the feet, that wiping may mean washing—because among the Arabs wiping is light washing? This has been related from Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī, who cited their expression, ‘I performed tamassaḥ for prayer,’ thus calling washing ‘wiping’; and on that basis some exegetes interpreted His saying, Exalted is He, ‘Then he began wiping the shanks and necks,’ meaning that he washed their shanks and necks. We say: this is false in several respects. Among them is that the possible lexical sense of a word is not authoritative when, in the convention of the Sacred Law, it is specialized for a single meaning. So even if we conceded that washing in the language can be called wiping, that would not undermine our interpretation of the verse, because the use of wiping in the Sacred Law conveys what washing does not convey. For this reason, the people of the Sacred Law designated some of the organs of purification as wiped and others as washed, distinguished between the two rulings, and differentiated between saying, ‘So-and-so holds that the obligation concerning the feet is wiping,’ and saying, ‘So-and-so holds washing.’ Another is that since the heads are wiped with a wiping that does not fall under the meaning of washing by consensus, and the feet are coordinated to them, it is necessary that their ruling be like the ruling of the heads in wiping and in its manner, because one who differentiates between them, despite the conjunction, in the manner of wiping is like one who differentiates between them in the wiping itself. Another is that if wiping were washing and washing were wiping, then the proof constantly cited by our opponents—namely, their report from him عليه السلام that he performed wudu (ablution) and washed his feet—would collapse, because it could not be denied that the washing mentioned there was only wiping. Thus, their interpretation of the verse on this basis invalidates the foundation of their own doctrine regarding washing the feet. Another is that the argument of those linguists who made wiping mean washing is based on washing containing wiping, but not everything that contains something else can validly be named by its name. We know that washing includes acts such as pressure and movement, yet it is not permissible to call it by the names of what it contains. As for Abū Zayd’s citation of their saying, ‘I performed tamassaḥ for prayer,’ its meaning is that when they wanted to express purification in a concise term, they could not say, ‘I washed myself for prayer,’ because purification includes what is not washing; and they found it lengthy to say, ‘I washed and wiped for prayer,’ so instead they said, ‘I performed tamassaḥ,’ because the washed limbs are also wiped. Thus they spoke figuratively for brevity, or relying on the meaning being understood. This does not require that they made wiping one of the names of washing. As for the verse, most exegetes interpreted it differently from what was mentioned in the question. Abū ʿUbaydah, al-Farrāʾ, and others said that the meaning of ‘then he began wiping’ is ‘striking’; others said it means actual wiping, namely that he wiped their manes and legs; while an anomalous group said that it meant washing. And whoever says that does not deny that interpreting wiping as washing is metaphorical and figurative; and we are not permitted to depart in the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, from the literal meaning to metaphor except in necessity.
“Then he began wiping the shanks and the necks.”

If it is said: Why do you deny that the genitive reading entails wiping, except that it relates to the khuffs and not to the feet, while the accusative reading entails washing that truly relates to the feet, so that the verse, by the two readings, would indicate both matters? We say: the khuff is not called a foot in language or in the Sacred Law, just as a turban is not called a head and a face-veil is not called a face. So if it were permissible to interpret what is mentioned in the verse concerning the feet to mean khuffs, then the same would be permissible in all the similar cases we mentioned. If it is said: Then what do you say about the reading with the feet in the accusative, which most reciters follow, and which necessitates washing and allows nothing else? We say: the first thing to note is that the genitive reading is agreed upon, while the accusative reading is disputed, because we say that the accusative reading is not permissible, and that the revealed reading is only the genitive reading; and that which indicates this is...

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation for protection; here, the context in which the report is interpreted
key_terms.الطَّهَارَةِ: ritual purity; the broader legal context of the discussion
key_terms.الْخُفَّيْنِ: the two leather socks; rejected here as the referent of the verse’s wording
key_terms.الْعَطْفِ: coordination by conjunction; used to argue that the feet share the ruling of the head
key_terms.الْغَسْلُ: washing; the alternative interpretation being refuted
key_terms.الْقِرَاءَةِ بِالْجَرِّ: the genitive reading of the verse; taken here as evidence for wiping
key_terms.الْمَسْحُ: wiping; the required act over the feet in wudu (ablution) according to the argument here
key_terms.الْمُجَاوَرَةِ: grammatical adjacency; an Arabic inflectional phenomenon argued here not to apply to the verse

ai.seo_question: Does the Quran require wiping or washing the feet in wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This passage argues that the report about immersing the feet is to be understood under taqiyyah, while the normative ruling in wudu (ablution) is wiping the feet. It then presents an extended grammatical and linguistic defense of reading the Quranic verse on wudu (ablution) as requiring wiping rather than washing, rejecting arguments based on adjacency in grammar or on treating wiping as a form of washing.
